title: Is AI Recommending Your Med Spa, or the One Down the Street?
seoTitle: Is AI Recommending Your Med Spa or a Competitor?
seoDescription: AI assistants name only a few med spas per answer. Here is how to check what ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Mode say about yours in 10 minutes.
excerpt: When a client asks AI for the best med spa near her, she usually gets a few names. Here is how to check whether yours is one of them, and what good looks like.
imageAlt: Woman in a white sweater sitting on a gray sectional sofa in a bright living room, looking at her phone with a focused expression
imageIdea: Real photo of a person checking a phone in a calm, stylish home setting, screen not readable, no clinical procedure and no brand logos.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
When someone asks ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity or Google's AI Mode for the best med spa near them, the answer usually names a small handful of businesses, not a page of ten links. If your med spa is not in that handful, the client may never see your name, and the practice down the street gets the consultation. You can check where you stand in about ten minutes, and this post shows you how.

This is not a reason to panic. But the shortlist is short, and it is worth knowing whether you are on it.

What happens when a client asks AI for the best med spa near them?

The assistant reads what it can find about local businesses, then writes a short answer with a few names. Some tools show their sources. Google's AI Mode can also show local business details such as ratings, reviews and hours, according to Google's announcement.

The key difference from a normal search is space. BrightLocal's study of about 200,000 unbranded local prompts found ChatGPT named an average of 4.1 businesses per response, Google AI Mode 3.5 and Google AI Overviews 2.5. That study covered local businesses in general, not med spas in particular, but the pattern is the point: a few names, and everyone else is left out of that answer.

Why does being left out matter?

Because more people are asking. In BrightLocal's 2026 survey of 1,002 U.S. adults, 45% of consumers said they had used ChatGPT or other AI tools for local business recommendations, and 31% had used ChatGPT for that in the last year. The same research found 42% of consumers trust AI recommendations as much as traditional reviews.

Picture a client looking for lip filler. She asks an assistant, gets three names, looks those up and stops there. She cannot choose a med spa she never hears about, and you will not see that lost visit in your analytics, because it never reached you.

The good news: the same BrightLocal study found only 20% to 33% average overlap between result sets when the same search was repeated. A med spa missing today is not locked out, and one named today should not assume it always will be.

How can you check what AI says about your med spa in 10 minutes?

Open each assistant in a private browser window, signed out where you can. Put your city or neighborhood in every question, because OpenAI's ChatGPT search help page says it estimates your general location from your IP address and suggests adding a city, neighborhood or postal code when local results look off.

Then ask the questions your clients ask, in their words. A few examples:

What to askWhat it tells you
Best med spa in [city] for a HydraFacialWhether you make the shortlist for a specific treatment
Who does natural looking lip filler near [neighborhood]?Whether you are linked to the results clients care about, in their language
Most trusted injector in [city]Which reputation signals the assistant leans on
Med spa near [neighborhood] open on SaturdaysWhether your hours and details are being read correctly
What do people say about [your med spa name]?Which reviews and themes get repeated about you

Run the same five questions in ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google. On Google, check both the regular results page, where an AI Overview may or may not appear, and AI Mode. For each answer, write down three things: whether you were named, which competitors were named, and which sources were shown. Perplexity says each answer includes numbered citations, and Gemini shows a Sources button when sources are available, so those two make tracing easiest.

What signals does AI seem to rely on?

No assistant publishes a full recipe. But public documentation and research point to a few signals that keep coming up.

  • Reviews. Google says on its local ranking help page that more reviews and positive ratings can help local ranking, and AI Mode displays ratings and reviews for local businesses.
  • Your own website. In BrightLocal's analysis of 800 ChatGPT local searches, business websites made up 58% of the sources ChatGPT showed, followed by business mentions at 27% and directories at 15%. If your site does not clearly say what you offer and where, there is less for an assistant to quote.
  • Clear service pages. A client asking about a HydraFacial or lip filler is asking about a treatment. A page that explains each treatment in plain language gives an assistant something specific to match. A single list of service names gives it very little.
  • Consistent details across the web. When your name, address, hours and phone number match on your website, Google Business Profile and directories, there is less room for an assistant to repeat the wrong version.
  • Third party mentions. Local press, "best of" lists and directory profiles are other places an assistant can find your name. The BrightLocal source analysis counted these business mentions as a separate category from your website.
  • Being readable at all. Google says a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, with no extra technical requirements. A treatment menu that lives only in a PDF or an image is harder to work with than plain text.

These are the same basics that help a client choose you once she finds you. We covered the full client journey in how clients choose a med spa online, and the Google side in our Google Business Profile checklist for med spas.

What does "good" look like?

Good does not mean appearing in every answer every time. Given how much answers move, nobody can honestly promise that. Good looks more like this:

  1. You show up for the treatments you most want to grow, at least some of the time, across more than one assistant.
  2. The facts are right. Your hours, location, providers and treatment list match what is true today.
  3. The description sounds like you. The themes an assistant repeats from your reviews are the ones you would want a new client to hear.
  4. Your own pages are among the sources. When citations are shown, your website or Google Business Profile appears, not only third party pages you do not control.
  5. You know who else is named. When a competitor shows up and you do not, you can see which sources the assistant used for them.

If your check shows the opposite, with wrong hours, a thin description or a competitor named for every treatment you offer, that is your starting point, not a verdict.

What should a med spa keep in mind about claims and privacy?

Two cautions. First, the words on your treatment pages may be quoted back to clients by an assistant, so they need to be accurate. The FTC's Health Products Compliance Guidance says health claims need competent and reliable scientific evidence. Have your medical director approve treatment descriptions, and avoid promising results.

Second, protect client privacy in everything you publish and in every review reply. If HIPAA applies to your practice, HHS says marketing uses of patient information generally require written authorization. Never confirm in public that someone was a client.

Questions we hear

Does ChatGPT recommend med spas?

Yes, if someone asks. ChatGPT can search the web and answer local questions, and BrightLocal's study of local prompts found it named an average of 4.1 businesses per response. That study covered local businesses in general, not med spas specifically.

Why does AI recommend a competitor and not my med spa?

Usually because the assistant found more, or clearer, information about them. Check which sources it cites for the competitor, then compare them with your own website, Google Business Profile, reviews and directory listings.

Can I pay to be recommended by ChatGPT or Google AI Mode?

Not in the organic answer. Google says there is no way to pay for a better local ranking, and its AI features draw on pages that are indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Ads are a separate product.

How often should I check what AI says about my med spa?

Monthly is a reasonable rhythm, and again after a change such as new treatments, new hours or a move. BrightLocal found answers to the same question often change on repeat searches, so look for patterns over time, not a single result.

takeaways: AI assistants usually name only a few businesses per answer: BrightLocal found ChatGPT averaged 4.1, Google AI Mode 3.5 and AI Overviews 2.5 in local prompts.
BrightLocal's 2026 survey found 45% of consumers used AI tools for local business recommendations, so being left out of the answer can quietly send clients to a competitor.
You can check in about 10 minutes: ask five client style questions with your city in ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google, and note who is named and which sources are shown.
Reviews, clear treatment pages, consistent details across the web and third party mentions are the signals that keep coming up.
Treatment descriptions should be accurate and approved by your medical director, and client privacy comes first in every page and review reply.
